name: Damasus of Rome
knownFor: Bishop of Rome from 366 or 367 after an election fought with clubs and swords, whose councils held to the creed of Nicaea, and who set Jerome of Strido to revise the Latin Gospels.
dates: Bishop from 366, by the Avellana account's date, or 367, by Jerome of Strido's Chronicle as A. C. Zenos cites it; died in the reign of Theodosius at almost eighty, by Jerome's account

keyWorks.title: Synodal letter to the bishops of Illyria
keyWorks.about: from a council at Rome, condemning Auxentius of Milan and holding to the creed of Nicaea; kept by Theodoret of Cyrus

keyWorks.title: Synodal letter against Apollinarius and Timothy
keyWorks.about: condemning Timothy, follower of Apollinarius of Laodicea, by the judgment of the apostolic see; kept by Theodoret

keyWorks.title: Confession of faith sent to Paulinus
keyWorks.about: a list of anathemas against Arius, Eunomius, Sabellius, Photinus and the Macedonians, among others; kept by Theodoret

traces: At his request Jerome of Strido revised the old Latin Gospels against the Greek. Jerome's preface begins, "You urge me to revise the old Latin version."
Jerome says that he helped Damasus with his letters and wrote his answers to the councils of the East and West.
remembered: Jerome, writing to him from the East in 376 or 377, said he kept communion with none but Damasus, "that is with the chair of Peter."
In his Lives of Illustrious Men, Jerome remembers that he "had a fine talent for making verses and published many brief works in heroic metre."

Ammianus Marcellinus, a historian and most likely a pagan, set the riot of his election beside a sharp picture of Rome's bishops, "enriched by offerings from matrons, riding in carriages, dressing splendidly."
Blomfield Jackson, who translated Theodoret, quotes Northcote and Brownlow on his work in the catacombs, "to rediscover the tombs which had been blocked up for concealment under Diocletian."

uncertain: Ammianus Marcellinus blames both rivals and counts a hundred and thirty-seven dead in the Basilica of Sicininus in one day. Socrates of Constantinople blames Ursinus, who had himself ordained in secret. Sozomen, a church historian of the fifth century, tells it the same way after him. An anonymous account from Ursinus's own party, kept in the Collectio Avellana, blames Damasus. It says he paid charioteers, arena men and gravediggers, and counts a hundred and sixty dead in a church he besieged, none on his side.

The Avellana account dates Liberius's death and the fighting by the consuls of 366, and Chester Hartranft, who translated Sozomen, dates Liberius's death to September 366. A. C. Zenos, who translated Socrates, notes that Jerome's Chronicle puts it in 367.

The chronological tables in W. H. Fremantle's translation of Jerome's works date his death to December 384. Ernest Cushing Richardson, who translated Jerome's Lives, gives 380 in a note. Jerome himself says only that he died under Theodosius, at almost eighty.
Zenos's note calls him "a Spaniard by race, native of Mantua". No early witness in the sources used here gives his birthplace.
Sozomen calls his rival Ursicius. Ammianus, Socrates and the Avellana account call him Ursinus.
